title: Kalanj
eyebrow: Anna's people, and the parish nobody has opened
dek: The family this archive's own great-great-grandmother came from — what can be proved about her, what two archives disagreed about, and the parish register that would answer it. The Kalanj genealogy proper is kept in The Blažević Archive; this page is the join, and the evidence on this side of it.
lead: David asked on 29 September 2026 whether Kalanj was a family this site should track and give a page of its own. It was — and building the page found a misreading this archive had carried in fifteen files, and a phrase in the same line of the same entry that no file carried at all. What follows is the evidence on this side of the join, in the order it was read: the baptism, the two things that baptism says which this archive had got wrong or missed, the stone the registers contradict, and eleven photographed graves that suggest a sibling set and cannot yet prove one.
source_kalanj: Ledenice baptismal register, entry 2 of 1864, read from the plate held here at 6×. David's photographs of the Kalanj graves, 29 September 2026. The Blažević Archive's Kalanj page, read 29 September 2026.

sections.h2: It begins with one line in a Vinodol baptism
paras: «Anna, legitima — **Josephus Kalanj et Rosalia nata Perković ejus uxor, Brinjensis Parochiæ ruricolæ**» — at «**Kljenovica N° 22**». Godparents Josephus Ban and his wife Anna; baptised by Vincentius Segulja, parish priest. The register of Ledenice, the Vinodol parish above Crikvenica. (**doc** — the plate is held here and was read at 6×.)

She married **Josip Defranceschi**, the stonecutter's son who brought this archive's line down from Gračišće to the coast, and she is **generation four of [the direct line](/direct-line/)**. Five children are recorded to the couple. Anton Rudolf's baptism is entry 9 of the Klenovica register for 1890; four further baptismal entries at Crikvenica name the mother **Ana Kalanj**, and those four entries are the reason the next section but two exists.

Two sentences of that one line turned out to be worth a section each. The first is a place name this archive had been reading wrongly since it first transcribed the entry. The second is four words nobody had transcribed at all.

sections.h2: How this household joins the Defranceschi line

sections.lab: Corrected 29 September 2026 · fifteen files, including the pedigree's own wall note
sections.h2: «Rijenovica» does not exist, and the mistake hid a fact
paras: Until today this archive read that place as «**Rijenovica** house 22» and said so in fifteen files. There is no Rijenovica. The word returns **zero hits** in this archive's Croatian gazetteer. The register says **KLJENOVICA** — the older spelling of **Klenovica** — and [the Blažević Archive](https://daviddef.github.io/TheBlazevic/kalanj/) has read it correctly all along.

What the misreading concealed is the part worth keeping. This site's [Crikvenica page](/crikvenica-house/) already said: «House 22 is somewhere in this line of roofs — **Anton Rudolf Defranceski was born in it on 20 January 1890**.» **Anna was born in the same house twenty-six years earlier.** The archive held «house 22» at both ends of the same family and never joined them, because at one end the village had the wrong name.
The correction is recorded on [corrections](/corrections/), and `check-propagation.py` now holds every file that asserted the old reading.

sections.lab: «Brinjensis Parochiæ ruricolæ» · four words later in the same line
sections.h2: And the same entry says where they came from, which no file of this archive carried
paras: **Country people of the parish of Brinje.** Not one file of this archive carried that phrase, and it is the most important thing in the entry: **the Kalanj were not coastal people.** Brinje is inland, up behind the Velebit gap; they had come down to Klenovica on the shore.

[The Blažević Archive](https://daviddef.github.io/TheBlazevic/kalanj/) calls Brinje «the single largest hole in this family» and records that «**not one page of its register has been opened**». So both archives now stand at the same closed door from opposite sides, and this page exists partly to say so out loud rather than leave each of them discovering it separately.

sections.h2: The oldest open question in this archive is a Kalanj question
paras: The registers name **ANA KALANJ** in all four Crikvenica baptismal entries of her children. The family's own genealogy gives Josip a wife **ANA GRUBIŠIĆ**, 19 September 1863 – 28 May 1936, and that is the name cut on the Crikvenica gravestone.

**The registers govern here and the stone is unexplained.** And the stone no longer exists: the plot was sold to the neighbour of the family house and the monument taken apart, so [the photograph of it](/crikvenica-house/) is now the only record there will ever be.

This is why Anna's page carries **no death date**. The only date on offer belongs to a name this archive cannot yet reconcile with hers, and borrowing it would be the kind of quiet join that the Rijenovica correction above exists to punish. (**open**)

sections.lab: Crikvenica, Novi Vinodolski and Klenovica · photographed 29 September 2026
sections.h2: Eleven stones, and a sibling set taking shape
paras: Eleven Kalanj monuments have been photographed in the three cemeteries and are held here as plates. Which of the three each stone stands in is not distinguished in the photographs and is not guessed.

subs.h3: Four of them cluster around Anna's own generation
paras: **LUKA KALANJ 1859–1944** and **KATA 1860–1942** on a ledger slab; and **ROZALIJA KALANJ 1865–1943**, whose first digit is damaged and was read at 5×. Anna was born in **1864**.

So there are Kalanj born in **1859, 1860, 1864 and 1865** in one small stretch of the Vinodol — and **Rozalija is the name of Anna's own mother**, Rosalia née Perković, which is exactly what a second daughter would be called. A sibling set is the obvious reading: Josip Kalanj and Rosalia's children, with one daughter named for her mother.

subs.h3: It is still a guess, and the test is cheap
paras: **No stone here names a father.** Four birth years in a six-year span, in three small cemeteries of one parish, with a shared given name, is proximity — and this archive has spent the day learning what proximity is worth without a document.

The test is specific and it is the most tractable question on this page: **the Ledenice baptisms of 1855–1870**, where Anna's own entry (number 2 of 1864) already sits, and where her brothers and sisters would sit within a few pages of her. (**open**)

Albert 1895–1945 with five of his household; Petar 1913–1971 and Vera 1917–2011 with the infant Milan 1943–1944; Mate 1928–1992; Franjo 1933–2004; a joint Kalanj–Rebrović stone; Vinko 1901–1961 and Paulina 1904–1984; Josip 1950–1983 with Franjo 1909–1991 and Zora 1923–1999; Tomislav 1935–2006; Judita 1934–2012 with Marijan 1931–2019; and Rozalija's own, with Anton 1897–1977, Marija 1898–1989 and Milan 1927–2006.

subs.h3: One stone carries the šahovnica, and nothing else here does
paras: **OBITELJ KALANJ — MARTIN 1905–1988 and MARTINA 1913–1995.** Two porcelain ovals, a stone cross standing in the gravel above — and propped against the plot, **a pink stone plaque cut with the Croatian chequy shield**.
It is the only national emblem on any stone in this whole set of photographs. It is worth recording as such and **nothing more**: a family put it there, and when or why is not on the stone.

subs.h3: Two photographs could not be stored
paras: They reached this archive inline rather than as files: **that one**, and **LOVRO 1906–1965** with Ana, Ivan and Marijan. They want re-sending if they are to be kept.

sections.lab: Four doors, and what is behind each
sections.h2: What is not known, and is worth asking for

asks.q: Are Luka, Kata and Rozalija Anna's brother and sisters?
asks.a: **Ledenice baptisms, 1855–1870.** Anna's own entry is number 2 of 1864 and has been read. Her siblings would sit within a few pages of it, naming the same father. This is the cheapest question on the page and the one that would turn four stones from proximity into a family.

asks.q: Where in Brinje do the Kalanj begin? — the door is now measured
asks.a:
**The Brinje registers ARE filmed, and they begin twenty-four years too late.** The Croatian State Archives' collection **HR-HDA-1448** holds Brinje under one name and one confession only: **births 1888–1892, 1893–1897 and 1897–1900; marriages 1888–1899; deaths 1888–1899** — reels **ZM-34C/681** and **ZM-34C/682**, topographic marks **M-1278** and **M-1279**, all of them **transcripts**, and **not one of them digitised**.

Anna was born in **1864** and her parents married before that, so **no filmed Brinje book can hold her baptism, her parents' marriage, or her brothers and sisters.** What is left is the reading room in Zagreb for 1888–1900, or the pre-1888 books wherever they survive — the parish office, the diocesan archive of Senj-Modruš, or the state archive at Gospić, none of which has been asked. [The full holding, with the ordering route.](/searched/)

asks.q: Who is the Ana Grubišić on the Crikvenica stone?
asks.a: The registers say Josip's wife was Ana Kalanj, four times. The stone said Ana Grubišić, 1863–1936. The stone is destroyed and the photograph is the record. Reconciling the two names is the oldest open question in this archive.
The šahovnica stone (Martin and Martina) and the Lovro 1906–1965 stone arrived inline and could not be stored. They are described here from the images as seen; they are not held.

sections.h2: Where the family itself is kept
paras: The Kalanj genealogy proper — **215 published people, earliest birth 1734**, running through Klenovica and Povile — is kept in [The Blažević Archive](https://daviddef.github.io/TheBlazevic/kalanj/), and is not rebuilt here. That boundary is right.

It had one cost, and this page is the answer to it: **while each archive read only its own page, the two of them held one baptism and disagreed about the village for months.** What belongs *here* is the join, the evidence photographed on this side, and the disagreements between the two. What belongs *there* is the family.
